front_blocks.md: Define **spin-spin splitting**.

back_blocks.md: A **spin-spin splitting** is the splitting of an NMR peak into sub-peaks caused by a proton's spin interacting with the spin states of protons on adjacent, non-equivalent carbons.

cards.back_md: A **spin-spin splitting** is the splitting of an NMR peak into sub-peaks caused by a proton's spin interacting with the spin states of protons on adjacent, non-equivalent carbons.

front_blocks.md: State the n+1 rule for <sup>1</sup>H NMR and explain what n represents.

back_blocks.md: The **n+1 rule** states that a proton with *n* protons on adjacent carbons splits into *n*+1 sub-peaks. **n** is the number of non-equivalent protons on the directly neighbouring carbon atom(s).

cards.front_md: State the n+1 rule for <sup>1</sup>H NMR and explain what n represents.
cards.back_md: The **n+1 rule** states that a proton with *n* protons on adjacent carbons splits into *n*+1 sub-peaks. **n** is the number of non-equivalent protons on the directly neighbouring carbon atom(s).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In <sup>1</sup>H NMR, equivalent protons cause spin-spin splitting of each other's signals.

back_blocks.md: **False.** **Equivalent protons** do **not** cause spin-spin splitting of each other's signals. Only non-equivalent protons on adjacent carbons cause splitting.

front_blocks.md: What information does the area under a peak in a <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum provide?

back_blocks.md: The **area under a peak** is proportional to the **number of protons** in that particular molecular environment, allowing the ratio of different types of hydrogen to be determined.

front_blocks.md: Define **molecular environment (****<sup>1</sup>****H NMR)**.

back_blocks.md: A **molecular environment** in <sup>1</sup>H NMR is the unique chemical surrounding of a proton; chemically equivalent protons share the same environment and produce a single peak at the same chemical shift.

cards.back_md: A **molecular environment** in <sup>1</sup>H NMR is the unique chemical surrounding of a proton; chemically equivalent protons share the same environment and produce a single peak at the same chemical shift.

front_blocks.md: In which chemical shift range would you expect the signal for a proton on a carbon adjacent to a C=O group?

back_blocks.md: Protons on a carbon adjacent to a **carbonyl group** (alkyl next to C=O) appear in the range **2.2–3.0 ppm**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
All four protons in 1,2-dichloroethane are in the same <sup>1</sup>H NMR environment and produce a single peak.

back_blocks.md: **True.** In **1,2-dichloroethane** (Cl–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–Cl), all four protons are chemically equivalent and produce **one singlet** on the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum.

front_blocks.md: Define **tetramethylsilane (TMS)**.

back_blocks.md: **Tetramethylsilane (TMS)** is Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>, used as the reference compound in NMR spectroscopy. Its single sharp peak is assigned a chemical shift of 0 ppm.

cards.back_md: **Tetramethylsilane (TMS)** is Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>, used as the reference compound in NMR spectroscopy. Its single sharp peak is assigned a chemical shift of 0 ppm.

front_blocks.md: Why does TMS produce only one sharp peak in an NMR spectrum, despite containing 12 hydrogen atoms?

back_blocks.md: All 12 hydrogen atoms in **TMS** are in the **same molecular environment** (four identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups bonded to Si), so they all absorb at the same frequency and produce one high-intensity peak.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
TMS is used as a reference in NMR because it is reactive and has a high boiling point.

back_blocks.md: **False.** **TMS** is used because it is **inert and volatile** — properties that prevent it from reacting with samples and allow easy removal after analysis.

front_blocks.md: Why is CDCl<sub>3</sub> preferred over an ordinary solvent when dissolving a sample for <sup>1</sup>H NMR?

back_blocks.md: **CDCl**<sub>**3**</sub> contains **deuterium (**<sup>**2**</sup>**H)** instead of hydrogen (<sup>1</sup>H). Deuterium absorbs radio waves in a different region, so the solvent peak does not interfere with the proton signals from the sample.

front_blocks.md: Define **deuterated solvent**.

back_blocks.md: A **deuterated solvent** is a solvent in which hydrogen atoms (<sup>1</sup>H) are replaced by deuterium (<sup>2</sup>H), preventing solvent peaks from interfering with the proton NMR signals of the dissolved sample.

cards.back_md: A **deuterated solvent** is a solvent in which hydrogen atoms (<sup>1</sup>H) are replaced by deuterium (<sup>2</sup>H), preventing solvent peaks from interfering with the proton NMR signals of the dissolved sample.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
After adding D<sub>2</sub>O to a sample, the –OH signal disappears from the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum.

back_blocks.md: **True.** Adding **D**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** causes the proton in **–OH** groups to exchange with deuterium, replacing <sup>1</sup>H with <sup>2</sup>H. The signal disappears because <sup>2</sup>H does not absorb in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR region.

front_blocks.md: Why can –OH and –NH peaks in <sup>1</sup>H NMR be difficult to identify without using D<sub>2</sub>O exchange?

back_blocks.md: **–OH** and **–NH** peaks are often **broad**, their chemical shift ranges can **overlap** with other proton types, and proton exchange with traces of water means only one average peak appears — making confident assignment difficult.
